meanings.note: Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to give', paired with 'давать'.

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'I', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'to you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?
And this is for you. A toy car!

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: Prefix 'пере-' denotes crossing over, repeating, or exceeding a limit (stem 'звонить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to call back', paired with 'перезванивать'.

examples.trans: A lucky break: Tretyakov called back.

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('glad').

examples.trans: I'm very glad to see you.

examples.text: Ну что ты? Я очень рад тебя видеть.
examples.trans: Oh, come on! I'm very glad to see you.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to see', paired with 'увидеть'.

examples.trans: I can see the toy car.

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.
See the markers? They're from Japan!

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'пасибо'). Common neuter noun meaning 'thank you' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'on, onto; for', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: The programme is on the website.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Prefix 'до-' marks reaching a boundary or finishing the remainder of an action (stem 'брый'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('kind; good').

examples.text: Добрый вечер, Вика. С Новым годом!
examples.trans: Good evening, Vika. Happy New Year!

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'лово'). Common neuter noun meaning 'word' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: А что я за мэр такой, который держит своё слово?
examples.trans: And what kind of mayor would I be if I kept my word?

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to joke', paired with 'пошутить'.

examples.text: Шутишь? Правда, скажи, где деньги? Меня наняли.
examples.trans: Are you joking? Seriously, tell me, where's the money? They hired me.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'how; as', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to feel', paired with 'почувствовать'.

examples.text: А с Пашей я снова чувствую себя женщиной.
examples.trans: And with Pasha I feel like a woman again.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'oneself', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: А с Пашей я снова чувствую себя женщиной.
examples.trans: And with Pasha I feel like a woman again.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'well; come on', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'this, that; it is', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: And this is for you. A toy car!

meanings.note: Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'quit, threw', paired with 'бросать'.

examples.text: Меня жена бросила. Два пальца сломаны.
examples.trans: My wife has left me. Two of my fingers are broken.

examples.text: Ну ладно, брось! Мы только поедим.
examples.trans: Oh come on, stop it! We'll only eat.

examples.text: А он тут, соседи сверху бросили. Уже месяц висит на улице!
examples.trans: It's right here, the upstairs neighbours threw it. It's been hanging outside for a month already!

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('newcomer').

examples.text: А вот это у нас новенький.
examples.trans: And this one here is our newcomer.
One moment, I ask for everyone's attention.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to be; there is'.

examples.trans: You will be asking for forgiveness.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'in, into', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'чало'). Common neuter noun meaning 'beginning' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: At the beginning of the week.

examples.text: Ваня, это теперь твоё. И это только начало.
examples.trans: Vanya, this is yours now. And it's only the beginning.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'century; age' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: The monastery is eight centuries old.
That was in the last century.

examples.text: Наш с вами город очень старый. Почти четыре века здесь были набеги.
examples.trans: Our town is very old. For almost four centuries there were raids here.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'work, job' in everyday Russian.
High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'after all, you know', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I did tell you, you know!

examples.text: Садись, не бойся. Я ведь сам чуть тебя не отпустил.
examples.trans: Sit down, don't be afraid. I very nearly let you go myself.

examples.text: Я ведь сам чуть тебя не отпустил.
examples.trans: I very nearly let you go myself.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'very, very much', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I love our town very much.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо сделать ещё больше.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need to do even more.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'not', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

выдавать.gloss: to hand out, pass off, betray

meanings.en: to hand out, pass off, betray
meanings.note: Prefix 'вы-' ('out of') marks outward movement or thorough completion (stem 'давать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to hand out, pass off, betray'.

examples.text: Он выдавал себя за другого человека.
examples.trans: He passed himself off as another person.

examples.text: Мне правда неловко выдавать себя за писателя.
examples.trans: I really feel awkward impersonating a writer.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'then, later, afterwards', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
Prefix 'об-' ('around, about') marks encirclement or comprehensive action (stem 'ъяснить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to explain', paired with 'объяснять'.

examples.trans: I will explain everything to you right now.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'at, by; (у меня) I have', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'restaurant' (from 'restaurer', to restore strength with rich broth); entered Russian in the early 19th century.

examples.trans: They called from the Italian restaurant.
In the evening they went to a restaurant.

examples.text: Кстати, звонили из итальянского ресторана. Дарят папе романтический ужин на двоих.
examples.trans: By the way, they called from the Italian restaurant. They're giving Dad a romantic dinner for two.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'no; there isn't', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
Common masculine noun meaning 'head chef, executive chef' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: The head chef manages the entire kitchen.

examples.text: Они привели нового шеф-повара прямо из Индии.
examples.trans: They brought a new chef straight from India.

examples.text: Шеф-повар решит, подходите ли вы ресторану.
examples.trans: The head chef will decide whether you suit the restaurant.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.
High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'from, out of', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Марина Сергеевна, я уже знаю. Мне звонили из мэрии.
examples.trans: Marina Sergeyevna, I already know. The town hall called me.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'paris' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: I still work as a cook.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'can, to be able', paired with 'смочь'.

examples.text: Этого не может быть. Это наша история.
examples.trans: That can't be. It's our history.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'oneself, myself, himself', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Я и сама хорошо проведу время.
examples.trans: I'll have a good time on my own.

examples.text: Николай Филиппович, простите меня, пожалуйста. Я сам не знаю, как это произошло.
examples.trans: Nikolai Filippovich, please forgive me. I don't know myself how it happened.

examples.text: Я сам не знаю, как это произошло.
examples.trans: I don't know myself how it happened.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'there', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'all, whole; everyone, everything', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

тереть.gloss: to rub, to scrub, to grate

meanings.en: to rub, to scrub, to grate
meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to rub, to scrub, to grate', paired with 'потереть'.

examples.trans: He tiredly rubbed his eyes with his hands.

examples.text: Аркашка, ты еле стираешь! Сильнее три!
examples.trans: Arkashka, you're barely washing! Rub harder!

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'person; (pl) people' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: There are a lot of people here.
I know the problems of ordinary people.
